title: Many people say Jesus received 39 lashes.
paragraphs: Many people say Jesus received 39 lashes.
But the truth is more sobering than that.
The Bible never tells us that Jesus was whipped 39 times.
That number comes from Jewish law.

In the Law of Moses, a guilty person could receive up to forty lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3). Jewish leaders later limited the punishment to “forty minus one”—39 lashes—to avoid accidentally exceeding the legal limit.
The apostle Paul even confirms this practice:

“Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one.”
— 2 Corinthians 11:24
But here is the detail many people miss.
Jesus was not scourged by Jewish authorities.
He was scourged by Romans.
And Roman soldiers did not follow the Jewish limit.
When the Roman governor Pontius Pilate handed Jesus over to be flogged, it was not a controlled religious punishment.
It was a Roman scourging.
And Roman scourging had no legal limit.
John 19:1 simply says:
“Then Pilate took Jesus and had Him flogged.”
No number.
No restraint.
No mercy.
Roman scourging was designed to break the body before crucifixion.
The whip often used was called a flagrum—a handle with several leather straps, embedded with pieces of bone, metal, or sharp fragments.
Every strike did more than bruise.
It tore.
It ripped.
It shredded flesh.
Victims were usually tied to a post with their backs exposed while soldiers struck repeatedly.
Historians record that some victims never survived the scourging itself.
Yet Jesus endured it.
Not because He was guilty.
But because He chose to stand in the place of sinners.
Centuries before this moment happened, the prophet Isaiah wrote words that would describe the suffering of the Messiah with stunning clarity:

“But He was pierced for our transgressions,
He was crushed for our iniquities;
the punishment that brought us peace was on Him,
and by His wounds we are healed.”
— Isaiah 53:5
Think about that.
Jesus did not just die for humanity.
He suffered for humanity.
Every wound carried meaning.
Every stripe carried purpose.
Every drop of blood testified to a love deeper than most people realize.
The soldiers who struck Him did not know they were fulfilling prophecy.
They thought they were punishing a criminal.
But heaven knew something else was happening.
The Lamb of God was carrying the weight of the world.
Isaiah also wrote:
Imagine the silence of that moment.
The Son of God—who could command angels—stood there and endured it.
No defense.
No retaliation.
No escape.
Why?
Because love was holding Him there.
The same Jesus who healed the sick.
The same Jesus who calmed storms.
The same Jesus who raised the dead.
Allowed Himself to be beaten by the very people He came to save.
And this is something worth remembering:
The suffering of Jesus was not an accident of history.
It was the plan of redemption.
Jesus Himself said in Mark 10:45:
“For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.”
The scourging was part of that ransom.
Part of the cost.
Part of the story of salvation.
But here is something powerful to consider.
The cross was not the end.
Three days later, the tomb was empty.
The wounds that once represented suffering became proof of victory.
After His resurrection, Jesus even showed those wounds to His disciples.
They were reminders that redemption had been accomplished.
The story of Jesus is not only about suffering.
It is about sacrifice, love, and resurrection power.
And maybe that is the deeper lesson hidden behind the question about the lashes.
The real point is not the number.
The real point is the love.
A love willing to endure unimaginable pain so that humanity could be reconciled to God.
A love that stepped into suffering so that others could receive grace.
A love that chose the cross.
So the next time you hear someone say Jesus received 39 lashes, remember this:
Scripture never gives a number.
But it does tell us something far more important.
He suffered.
He endured.
He gave Himself.
And He did it willingly.
For us.

“For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God.”
— 1 Peter 3:18
That is the story behind the stripes.
And that is the love behind the cross.
Reflection Question

When you think about what Jesus endured before the cross…
what does His sacrifice mean personally to you today?
